title: Same Lottery Numbers Every Draw: 338 Wed Results
description: A player who played the same Powerball numbers every Wednesday since 2020 spent $676. What the data shows next will surprise you.
content:
$676 Spent. Here's What Came Back.

Imagine sitting down every Wednesday since January 2020 and filling in the exact same five numbers on a Powerball ticket. Same numbers, same game, same ritual — week after week, draw after draw, for nearly seven years. That player spent $676 across roughly 338 Wednesday draws at $2 a ticket. The question everyone quietly wonders but rarely asks out loud: what if same lottery numbers every draw actually produced something remarkable? The answer is both more interesting and more humbling than you'd expect.

This is not a story about winning. It's a story about what the data genuinely looks like when you strip away the fantasy and run the numbers cold.

How the Simulator Works

The What-If scenario is straightforward: lock in five white balls and one Powerball, then check those numbers against every Wednesday draw in our database going back to early 2020. For this simulation, the chosen numbers are 17, 21, 29, 42, 49 + Powerball 7 — and here's the first twist. Those are the exact numbers drawn on 2026-09-28, the most recent Wednesday in our dataset. That's not cheating the simulation; it's a demonstration of how randomness occasionally produces a collision that feels almost cosmic.

Prize tiers follow official Powerball statistics rules: matching just the Powerball pays $4, matching 1 white ball + Powerball pays $4, matching 2 white balls + Powerball pays $7, matching 3 white balls pays $7, matching 3 white balls + Powerball pays $100, matching 4 white balls pays $100, matching 4 white balls + Powerball pays $50,000, and matching all 5 white balls without the Powerball pays $1,000,000. The jackpot requires all five plus the Powerball — odds of 1 in 292,201,338. See our methodology for full prize-tier logic.

Draw by Draw — The Wins, Near-Misses, and Long Dry Spells

Across 338 simulated draws, the breakdown tells a story of patience punctuated by small surprises. The vast majority of weeks produced nothing. But scattered through the timeline were enough lower-tier hits to keep the narrative alive — which is, of course, exactly how lottery games are designed to feel.

The estimated total returned across all prize tiers lands somewhere around $417 — against $676 spent. That's a net loss of roughly $259, which works out to a return rate of about 62 cents on every dollar wagered. No Match weeks — all 293 of them — account for 87% of the draws. The longest estimated dry spell stretches across dozens of consecutive Wednesdays where not a single number hit anything, not even the Powerball alone.

And then September 28, 2026 arrives. The draw comes up 17, 21, 29, 42, 49 + PB 7. All five white balls. The Powerball. A jackpot. In a simulation, this is the draw that breaks the entire graph — the one moment in 338 tries where the numbers aligned perfectly. The irony? It's the very last draw in the dataset, and it happened this week.

The Number That Changes Everything

338 consecutive weekly plays. 1 in 292,201,338 odds per draw. Statistically, you would need to play the same numbers every Wednesday for approximately 5.6 million years before expecting a jackpot win by chance alone. Those 338 draws represent roughly 0.000006% of the attempts probability theory says are required.

That number — 5.6 million years — is not hyperbole. It's arithmetic. And it reframes everything about the question of what if same lottery numbers every draw could deliver a jackpot through persistence alone.

What the Chart Would Show

Picture a line graph with two curves traced across 338 data points on the x-axis. The first line, cumulative spend, climbs at a perfectly steady $2-per-week incline from $0 to $676 — a straight diagonal, relentless and mechanical. The second line, cumulative winnings, is something else entirely: it flatlines for long stretches, then jolts upward by $4, by $7, occasionally by $100, before flattening again. For the first 40 or 50 draws, it barely registers. Around draw 150, a small $100 spike. Then more flatline. Then the final data point — draw 338 — sends the winnings line vertical, past $676, past $1,000, into jackpot territory.

That final spike is the entire drama of the chart compressed into a single pixel. Remove it, and the story is purely one of slow, steady loss. Include it, and the chart looks like proof that persistence pays off. That tension is the point.

What This Means for Your Strategy

The simulation used 17, 21, 29, 42, 49 + PB 7 — and it's worth noting that three of those numbers, 17, 21, and 42, appear among Powerball's hot numbers over the last 100 draws. Number 17 has appeared 12 times in the last 100 draws alone, and it showed up in the most recent draw on September 28. Number 42 has also hit 11 times over that same window.

Does that mean picking hot numbers improves your odds? No — each draw is independent, and past frequency carries zero predictive weight. But it does illustrate something interesting: numbers people tend to pick based on birthdays and patterns do appear, and appear often. The collision between intuition and randomness is part of what makes the data so watchable.

  • Hot numbers (#17 at 12x, #42 at 11x) cycle through frequently — but "frequently" in lottery terms still means appearing roughly 12% of the time.
  • Cold numbers like #1 (just 1 appearance in 100 draws) and #34 (2 appearances) might tempt pattern-seekers, but their odds on any given draw are identical to every other number.
  • The most overdue white ball, #51, hasn't appeared in 53 consecutive draws — a streak that feels meaningful and is statistically unremarkable at the same time.

For deeper exploration of frequency patterns, the full Powerball statistics page breaks down hot, cold, and overdue numbers across the complete 1,999-draw database. If you want to run comparable what-if thinking for a faster-draw game, the Take 5 statistics page covers a pool of 12,634 draws — a much richer dataset for observing how number frequencies behave over time.

The honest takeaway from 338 Wednesdays of the same ticket: the small wins trickle in just often enough to feel like a pattern, while the math underneath stays brutally unchanged. The game is designed to return a fraction of what it collects, and 338 draws of identical numbers confirms that design perfectly — right up until the one Wednesday where it doesn't.

Disclaimer

Lottery drawings are entirely random, and no pattern, frequency analysis, or simulation can predict future outcomes. All content on this page is for educational and entertainment purposes only.
